questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why a nested power becomes one power
questions.stem: Note 304 asks for an explanation of why 7 to the power 2 raised to the power 3 is written as 7 to the power 6 in the glossary.

answer.exemplar: A power of a power means the base is multiplied by itself as many times as the inner exponent says, and then that whole product is raised to the outer exponent, which multiplies the number of copies again. Seven to the power 2 is seven multiplied by itself twice, and raising that to the power 3 repeats the whole group three times, giving six copies of seven in total. That is exactly what 7 to the power 6 records, so the two notations agree.

questions.explanation: The inner exponent counts the copies of the base, and the outer exponent says how many times that group repeats, so the copies multiply to 6. The single-power notation records the same number of copies of 7.
questions.hint: Count the total copies of the base in the product.

questions.topic: Exponent produced by a nested power
questions.learningObjective: explain how a stack of powers becomes a single power
questions.stem: Note 310 asks for an explanation of why a stack of powers such as 2 to the power 3 raised to the power 2 raised to the power 4 is written as a single power of 2.

answer.exemplar: Each layer of the stack multiplies the number of copies of the base, because raising a power to a power repeats the entire group below it. The inner power of 3 gives three copies of 2, the next layer repeats that group twice for six copies, and the outer layer repeats those six copies four times for twenty-four copies in total. So the whole stack is 2 to the power 24, and the single exponent is the product of the layer exponents 3, 2, and 4.

questions.explanation: Every layer multiplies the count of copies of the base, so the exponent is the product of the layer exponents. Adding them would understate the size of the number the expression describes.
questions.hint: The exponent is the product of all the layers.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why a power of a product raises each factor
questions.stem: Note 316 asks for an explanation of why 4 times 6, raised to the power 2, equals 4 to the power 2 times 6 to the power 2.

answer.exemplar: Squaring a product means multiplying the product by itself, so 4 times 6 times 4 times 6 can be regrouped as 4 times 4 times 6 times 6, and each pair of like factors gives one square. That regrouping is valid because multiplication can be rearranged, and it shows the expression equals 16 times 36, which is 576, the same value as squaring 24 directly. The rule works for any power and any number of factors, and it is why exponents in expanded form always match the outer power.

questions.explanation: Regrouping the repeated product pairs each factor with itself, which produces one square of each factor. That is why 4 times 6 raised to the 2 equals 4 to the 2 times 6 to the 2.
questions.hint: Regroup the product into pairs of like factors.

questions.stem: Note 328 asks for an explanation of why the square root of 49 can be written as 49 to the power one half.

answer.exemplar: A fractional exponent of one over two asks for the number whose second power is 49, which is the definition of a square root, and the usual square root of 49 is 7 because 7 squared is 49. Writing the root as 49 to the power one half therefore means exactly the same thing as writing the root symbol, and the notation lets roots sit inside larger expressions where the symbol would be awkward. The exponent form also makes it clear that the index of the root becomes the denominator of the fraction.

questions.explanation: One half as an exponent asks for the number whose square is 49, which is the definition of the square root. The fractional form lets roots combine with other powers, which the symbol cannot easily do.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I

answer.exemplar: Combining radicals means adding like terms, and like terms must share the same radical part, not merely look similar. In the first sum both terms carry the square root of 3, so the coefficients add and give 7 times the square root of 3. In the second sum the second term carries the square root of 6, which is a different number from the square root of 3, so no like parts exist and the terms must stay separate. Simplifying first would not help, because the square root of 6 has no square factor to pull out.

questions.explanation: Like terms need the same radical part, and only the first sum has two terms with the square root of 3, so its coefficients combine into 7. The second sum has two different radical parts, so the terms stay separate.
questions.hint: Check whether the radical parts match exactly.
